narrative:
The model predicted a 56.1% chance that you would fail the bar exam on your first attempt. Because this probability tipped above 50%, the admissions system automatically rejected your law school application.

Three factors drove this outcome, ranked by importance. Your class ranking in the third year of law school was the strongest influence, pushing the prediction strongly toward failure. Being in the bottom decile (1 out of 10) placed you far below the average ranking of accepted students, who typically sit around the middle of their class. This low standing signaled to the model a higher risk of struggling with the bar exam.

Your undergraduate GPA worked in the opposite direction. At 3.40 it sits above the 3.23 average of accepted students, giving the model some reassurance that you have solid academic ability and slightly lowering the predicted risk of failure.

Your first-year class ranking came in third. Like your third-year rank, you placed in the lowest decile, well below the average of 6 for accepted students. This again pulled the prediction toward failure, though less forcefully than your later ranking.

Taken together, the model saw your consistently low class standing as outweighing your stronger college grades. To improve your chances, focus on raising your academic performance in law school so that your class rank moves closer to the middle or higher. Stronger rankings in future semesters, combined with targeted bar-prep work, would likely shift future predictions in your favor.
